articles.title: Enchente no Himalaia faz mais de 1,2 mil mortos e 5 mil desaparecidos | G1
articles.standfirst: Desastre provocado pelo colapso de uma geleira atingiu áreas da fronteira entre os dois países na semana passada
articles.summary: Desastre provocado pelo colapso de uma geleira atingiu áreas da fronteira entre os dois países na semana passada
articles.body:
As enchentes devastadoras na fronteira entre China e Nepal da última semana deixaram pelo menos 1.280 mortos e 5.624 desaparecidos , somando-se os dados das autoridades de gestão de desastres dos dois países nesta quinta-feira (3).

A imprensa estatal chinesa informou que 21 pessoas morreram no Tibete e que outras 541 estão desaparecidas. Já no Nepal, foram registradas 1.259 vítimas fatais e 5.083 paradeiros.

O desastre começou na última quarta-feira (26) , quando parte de uma geleira próxima ao pico Langtang Lirung, no Nepal, desabou. A queda arrastou grandes volumes de gelo e rochas e provocou uma avalanche que atingiu o rio Lhende Khola.

O material bloqueou o curso do rio e formou uma enorme onda de lama, pedras, gelo e água. O fluxo avançou por mais de 20 quilômetros e atingiu áreas do Nepal e do Tibete, destruindo vilarejos, estradas, pontes e instalações de energia.

Um dos locais mais atingidos foi o posto de fronteira de Gyirong, no Tibete. Imagens de câmeras de segurança registraram a força da enxurrada, que arrastou construções e pessoas. O local é uma importante ligação comercial entre a China e o Nepal.

Socorristas carregam corpos de vítimas das enchentes para um sepultamento coletivo em Chitwan, no Nepal — Foto: Nisha Shrestha / AP

articles.title: Por que o turismo compartilhado é perfeito para quem ama viver bem? | G1
articles.standfirst: Entenda como funciona a divisão de semanas entre proprietários, o que cada família recebe em troca e por que o modelo dá previsibilidade às férias de todo ano.
articles.summary: Entenda como funciona a divisão de semanas entre proprietários, o que cada família recebe em troca e por que o modelo dá previsibilidade às férias de todo ano
articles.body:
Por que o turismo compartilhado é perfeito para quem ama viver bem? — Foto: Crédito: Divulgação.

É mais simples do que parece. Essa expressão “turismo compartilhado” circula cada vez mais em conversas sobre viagem, mas nem sempre vem acompanhada de explicação. A ideia por trás dela é simples e antiga: dividir entre várias famílias o custo de um bem que uma só usaria por poucas semanas ao ano.

Aplicada ao lazer, essa lógica deu origem ao que o mercado chama de multipropriedade e o GR Group prefere chamar de Casa de Férias, porque é assim que o cliente vive o produto.

O ponto de partida é um imóvel real, dentro de um empreendimento de lazer, com unidade identificada e endereço. Em vez de comprar o apartamento inteiro, a família adquire uma fração dele e, com ela, o direito de usar a unidade em períodos definidos, todos os anos.

A distribuição desses períodos segue um sistema rotativo de semanas, organizado em faixas de temporada, como altíssima, alta e média. O rodízio existe justamente para que os períodos mais disputados circulem entre os proprietários ao longo dos anos, em vez de ficarem sempre com os mesmos.

A aquisição é formalizada em escritura, e a fração passa a integrar o patrimônio da família, podendo ser transmitida aos herdeiros. Como todo imóvel, também tem obrigações: há rateio das despesas de manutenção e operação do empreendimento, além dos tributos aplicáveis, tudo previsto em contrato, que vale a pena verificar na íntegra no momento de adquirir.

O empreendimento é operado por uma equipe de hotelaria, então o proprietário não administra nada. Não contrata manutenção, não cuida da limpeza e não se preocupa com a unidade fora da sua semana. Chega com a mala e encontra tudo pronto, como em um hotel.

Como a conta desta Casa de Férias é fracionada, o padrão do imóvel e da área de lazer costuma ser superior ao que uma família alcançaria sozinha em uma segunda casa: piscinas, gastronomia, atividades para crianças e serviços de hotel fazem parte do mesmo endereço.

Além de tudo isso, empreendimentos do grupo são associados à RCI Weeks, rede de intercâmbio de semanas presente em mais de 100 países e mais de 4.300 empreendimentos, e proprietários também podem ter acesso ao Mydest, o Clube de Férias do GR Group, de acordo com contrato vigente.

Existe ainda um ganho menos visível, e que costuma pesar para quem tem rotina apertada: a previsibilidade. Sem casa de férias, cada ano recomeça a mesma discussão. Para onde ir, quanto vai custar, se ainda há vaga no período em que a família consegue sair.

Com ela, essa decisão foi tomada uma vez. O destino está definido, o período é conhecido e a hospedagem das próximas temporadas já está resolvida. Sobra energia para a parte boa, que é planejar o que fazer quando chegar lá.

A relação de empreendimentos com casa de férias, com a descrição de cada destino e das modalidades disponíveis, está no site institucional . O grupo publica novidades no Instagram @grgroupbr e no LinkedIn /grgroup.

Para entender o modelo em detalhe, conhecer uma unidade e esclarecer dúvidas sobre escritura, rateio de despesas e regras de uso, a orientação é procurar a equipe pelos canais oficiais de atendimento ou agendar uma visita ao empreendimento de interesse.

articles.title: Acidente na Raposo Tavares em Ourinhos interdita trecho da rodovia  | G1
articles.standfirst: Colisão lateral aconteceu na manhã desta quinta-feira (3), no km 382, após um dos veículos acessar a via sem observar o tráfego. Apesar das faixas bloqueadas, ninguém ficou ferido.
articles.summary: A colisão entre carretas no km 382 da Raposo Tavares em Ourinhos bloqueou as faixas nesta quinta-feira, mas não houve registro de vítimas no local.
articles.body:
Acidente envolvendo duas carretas deixou a SP-270, na altura do km 382, totalmente interditada na manhã de quinta-feira (3), em Ourinhos (SP) — Foto: CCM - Artesp/Divulgação

Um acidente envolvendo duas carretas deixou a Rodovia Raposo Tavares (SP-270) na altura do km 382, totalmente interditada na manhã de quinta-feira (3), em Ourinhos (SP).

De acordo com informações da Agência de Transportes do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp), o motorista de uma das carretas, ao acessar o eixo principal da rodovia, entrou na rodovia sem observar o tráfego.

O motorista da outra carreta, que vinha logo atrás, não teve tempo de desviar ou frear, ocasionando uma colisão lateral.

Os dois veículos ficaram imobilizados sobre as duas faixas da rodovia e não houve registro de feridos. Todas as faixas e o acostamento foram liberados por volta das 11h.

articles.title: Ministro israelense apresenta plano para retirar palestinos de Gaza | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro de extrema direita propõe expulsar 250 mil palestinos em um ano e retirar os demais moradores do território nos seis anos seguintes
articles.summary: Ministro de extrema direita propõe expulsar 250 mil palestinos em um ano e retirar os demais moradores do território nos seis anos seguintes
articles.body:
Ministro israelense Itamar Ben-Gvir já publicou um vídeo feito por IA celebrando fome de prisioneiros palestinos em prisões do país. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O ministro da Segurança Nacional de Israel, Itamar Ben Gvir, apresentou nesta quinta-feira, 3, um plano para retirar os palestinos da Faixa de Gaza e enviá-los para o exterior .

Ben Gvir, do partido de extrema direita Poder Judaico, propõe a expulsão de 250 mil palestinos de Gaza em um ano . Os cerca de dois milhões de habitantes restantes desse território, devastado pela guerra entre Israel e o grupo islamista Hamas, deixariam a região nos seis anos seguintes.

"É realista", declarou o ministro, membro da coalizão governista e alvo frequente de críticas internacionais.

Ele também afirmou que diversos países estão "dispostos" a acolher os habitantes de Gaza, sem especificar quais.

articles.title: Comércios da Região Oeste de BH sofrem com falta de água  | G1
articles.standfirst: Intermitência no fornecimento forçou o fechamento temporário de uma academia no bairro Buritis.
articles.summary: Copasa prevê normalização do sistema apenas no sábado.
articles.body:
Além de casas e prédios, alguns pontos comerciais da região Oeste de Belo Horizonte continuam sem água nesta quinta-feira (03).

O desabastecimento, que já dura quase duas semanas, virou um transtorno na rotina de muitos belorizontinos.

A Copasa têm emitido boletins diários da Copasa sobre o status de fornecimento. (confira mais abaixo o boletim desta manhã)

Em uma academia localizada no bairro Burutis, o banheiro que é utilizado por alunos para banhos após atividades físicas, precisou ser interditado. Já a falta de água nos bebedouros, foi suprida com galões.

Thiago Oliveira, que é sócio do estabelecimento, conta que chegou a cogitar contratar um caminhão-pipa, mas descartou a mediada devido ao preço inflacionado durante o desabastecimento.

"O preço na região tá ficando em torno de R$ 3.500 reais. Então é inviável a compra de caminhão-pipa" afirma.

Ele ainda conta que a instabilidade no fornecimento tem impactado na no funcionamento da academia e frequência de alunos.

É complicado, porque você fica sem poder dizer para o aluno quando que vai ter água de fato, quando que ele pode se dispor a vir, porque a minha reserva dentro de uma loja dessa é pequena para suprir a necessidade dos alunos. Então não dá para ter uma certeza de atendimento de qualidade, né?", finaliza.

O desabastecimento aconteceu após o rompimento de uma adutora de grande porte , na Rua Xapuri, no bairro Nova Granada, no dia 19 de agosto.

Na ocasião, a força da água atingiu a região, chegou à Avenida Barão Homem de Melo e comprometeu o abastecimento de 33 bairros da capital.

Nesta segunda-feira (31), a Copasa iniciou uma obra emergencial para remanejar o trecho obstruído. Em nota, a companhia informou que a previsão de conclusão é até este sábado (05) .

Nos bairros Havaí e Betânia, equipes técnicas da Companhia seguem atuando para consolidar a recuperação do abastecimento nas áreas de maior altitude que são, historicamente, mais suscetíveis a oscilações de pressão.

Segundo a Copasa, 30 caminhões-pipa estão atuando em rotas prioritárias para abastecimento emergencial de hospitais, unidades de saúde, creches e escolas na região.

articles.title: National Memorial Arboretum's name change faces veterans' backlash
articles.summary: The site in Staffordshire will be renamed the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens.
articles.body:
National Memorial Arboretum's name change this month has been called "diminishing" and "unnecessary" by some visitors, including veterans.

Plans for the new name, Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens, were announced in April. The armed forces charity said it was to reflect the arboretum's full integration with RBL and broaden public engagement.

About 25,000 people signed a petition against the move, including Royal Air Force veteran Paul Cornhill, who visits the site in Alrewas, Staffordshire, to remember his stillborn daughter.

"I've decided it's a step too far to change the name to what they want," said Cornhill, from Tamworth, vowing not to attend future Remembrance services.

There are 420 memorials at the 150-acre site, which honours the service and sacrifice of the armed forces, emergency services and other civilian organisations, including the Sands charity's baby loss memorial.

Cornhill said enduring the loss of a stillborn baby had been difficult, but he described the Sands memorial as "a good place to go for a think and sit down and talk and have a bit of a cry even".

The petition claimed the arboretum's name change "undermines its rich heritage and the deep emotional connections many have with it".

David Willis, a Royal Navy veteran of 39 years from Polesworth, Warwickshire, said he visits to remember patients he treated as a medic.

"There are a lot of names of friends and former colleagues on the walls.

"There are also names of patients, I remember their names, on the walls as well, who we battled to save their lives but unfortunately passed away.

"Quite often I just touch their names when I'm there. It gives me comfort," he said.

And added: "To change it to 'memorial gardens' hasn't got that grandeur."

Stevan Jackson, a Royal Navy veteran of 35 years, said: "Branding the arboretum with Royal British Legion imposes a service-centric focus, which I think diminishes those other organisations and charities that are not service related but are represented at the arboretum.

"I don't see it as being at all necessary," added Jackson from Kidderminster, Worcestershire.

John Woodall from Stourbridge, West Midlands, said: "It's lost its emphasis as a national memorial for all services, whether they're public services, police, paramedics, or whoever, and obviously some private services."

The arboretum is visited by more than 300,000 people every year, including 26,000 young people on educational trips.

In a previous statement, the Royal British Legion said: "The naming process included research and consultation with members of the public… members of the Armed Forces community, volunteers, and staff."

But in a more recent statement, the charity said no formal consultation had taken place and that the decision was made "in line with established governance procedures and with scrutiny and approval from the Board of Trustees".

A spokesperson for Royal British Legion said: "RBL has provided stewardship to the Arboretum for 23 years, and during that time the charity has invested more than £34 million into enhancing facilities and ensuring entry remains free.

"The Arboretum's long-term future has been secured through full integration with RBL, and every decision has been taken in the interests of the estate and all those who care deeply about it.

"The decision to rename the site has been made, and work to implement the new name is in its final stages.

"The elements that make this place so special – the range of memorials and the inspirational stories behind them – will not change and will be protected by RBL for generations to come."

articles.title: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right
articles.summary: As Meta settled for up to $17 billion over claims its platforms harmed children, Hasidic smartphone restrictions started looking less backward.
articles.body: The irony was hard to miss last week. The same day that a documentary (with more than 35 million views as of Sept. 2) portrayed Hasidic restrictions on smartphones and the internet as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a proposed settlement worth up to $17 billion with a coalition of states over allegations that Facebook and Instagram harmed children through addictive design. Meta denies wrongdoing. As a kid, I spent enormous amounts of time outdoors, growing up near the Santa Monica Mountains and later in the rural mountains of Tehachapi, California. I explored the hills, watched wildlife, fished, stared at the stars, listened to coyotes howl and loved sleeping outside so much that sending me indoors for the night was my punishment. Try that punishment on a child with a smartphone today. A bedroom can contain a universe more compelling than anything outside: social media, YouTube, video games, group chats and an infinite stream of entertainment engineered to keep us hooked. When our oldest daughter was one year old, she became so attached to her iPad Mini that she’d shake her crib, crying, "iPad! iPad! iPad!" when we took it away. WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO In his documentary, Turkish filmmaker Ruhi Çenet takes viewers inside Hasidic communities in New York. Again and again, their distance from modern technology helps establish just how unusual and insular their world appears. "Have you ever watched television?" Çenet asks one man. "Have you ever logged into the internet in your entire life?" He learns that some members regard unrestricted internet access as dangerous to religious life. Some use "kosher" phones stripped of texting, web browsers and social media. Computers needed for work use filters restricting which websites users can visit. Instead of mainstream social media, some communities maintain telephone networks where people listen to stories, religious teachings and inspirational content. Looking at one kosher phone, Çenet marvels: "There’s no way to send SMS. No way to search anything. It’s like a walkie-talkie." Later, he remarks, "It feels like I traveled back in time," his stunned tone framing these restrictions as inherently negative. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIAL MEDIA ADDICTION WILL EASILY OUTLAST META'S MASSIVE MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR SETTLEMENT Then, on the same day that viewers of Çenet’s documentary encountered religious restrictions on technology as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a settlement, still subject to court approval, that would impose restrictions of its own, including a default daily limit for teens, blocking access overnight and adopting other safeguards aimed at reducing compulsive use. Perhaps the remarkable thing about a phone that "only makes calls" isn’t how little it can do. Perhaps it’s how little it can do to you. BIG TECH IS THROUGH HARMING OUR CHILDREN. THIS IS OUR TIME TO FIGHT BACK We routinely describe communities such as the Amish and some Jewish, Christian and Muslim groups as insular because they resist technologies that everyone else embraces. Last week, for instance, California’s Catholic bishops backed AB 1709, legislation that would restrict covered platforms from providing addictive features to children under 16. While the legislation has not yet become law, that resistance can still look irrational from the outside. Why reject a device capable of placing nearly all human knowledge in your pocket? AS AI RESHAPES DATING, A JEWISH ORGANIZATION IS BETTING ON THE RETURN OF THE HUMAN MATCHMAKER Of course, practices vary enormously. Some communities heavily restrict internet access; Chabad Lubavitch, the Hasidic movement with which I identify, embraces the internet as a tool for Jewish education and outreach. For roughly 25 hours every week, my phone stops buzzing. Emails wait. Work stops. In our hyperconnected world, deliberately making yourself unreachable sounds restrictive. I experience it as freedom. The lesson isn’t that these communities discovered the perfect technologies to prohibit. It’s that they believed they had the right to ask what technology would do to them before adopting it. 'IF WI-FI WENT OUT TOMORROW – CHAOS': AMERICAN ADDICTION TO TECHNOLOGY EXPLORED ON 'PLANET TYRUS' Modern America mostly reversed the process. We asked what technology could do for us first and worried about what it was doing to us later. We handed children extraordinarily sophisticated attention-capturing machines and then seemed surprised when they struggled to put them down. IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT? The U.S. Surgeon General’s office now calls harm from screen use among children and adolescents a public-health concern. Recent research has linked smartphone and screen use to depression, insufficient sleep and other adverse health outcomes. A 2026 Pediatrics study of 10,588 U.S. children found that smartphone ownership at age 12 was associated with higher odds of depression, obesity and insufficient sleep, although it’s important to note that the observational study could not establish causation. Researchers continue to debate causation, individual vulnerability and which forms of screen use cause the greatest harm. But handing children unrestricted access to products deliberately engineered to capture attention amounted to an enormous social experiment. PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US And we ran the experiment before knowing the results. Now mainstream society is trying to recreate boundaries that traditional communities never abandoned. Phone-free schools. Devices outside bedrooms. Parental controls. Delayed smartphones. Screen-time limits. Social media age restrictions. Notifications disabled overnight. Practices that once looked like symptoms of religious insularity have acquired respectable secular names: digital wellness, screen hygiene and intentional technology. Insularity carries genuine dangers. Communities that severely restrict outside information can suppress dissent, conceal abuse and limit access to ideas and opportunities. We should never romanticize that. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But isolation and restraint are not the same thing. The Amish preserve face-to-face communal life and manual work. Hasidic communities center life heavily around family, synagogue, schools, religious study and communal gatherings. Orthodox Judaism gives me something even more radical: Shabbat. For roughly 25 hours every week, my phone stops buzzing. Emails wait. Work stops. In our hyperconnected world, deliberately making yourself unreachable sounds restrictive. I experience it as freedom. We tend to define technological freedom as more access, information, entertainment and choice. But the freedom to be unavailable is another kind of freedom. To be bored. To sit through dinner without checking who texted. To walk through the woods. To let children experience an afternoon without an algorithm deciding what should capture attention. I don’t want to abandon modernity. Technology allows me to work, learn and maintain relationships in ways my grandparents could scarcely have imagined. The lesson isn’t to become Amish or Hasidic. It is to start with a hierarchy of values such as family, faith and community, and then ask where technology fits. Today, parents often fight the opposite battle: getting children to put down their devices and walk outside. For years, we looked at people without smartphones and wondered what they were missing. Perhaps we should have spent more time asking what they were preserving. Not every boundary is a prison. Sometimes it protects what matters most. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ELI FEDERMAN

articles.title: When gunman forced his way into Virginia elementary school, superintendent says lockdown procedures worked
articles.summary: Waynesboro police say a 19-year-old gunman entered Westwood Hills Elementary School and injured a staff member before school lockdown procedures kicked in.
articles.body: A 19-year-old gunman got inside a Virginia elementary school about 30 miles west of Charlottesville on Wednesday morning, injuring an adult staff member before turning the gun on himself, authorities said during a press conference later that day. The subject, Anthony Ignatiadis-Isabelle, was found "dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound," Waynesboro Police Chief David Shaw said. His body was found inside the library of Westwood Hills Elementary School, and no students were inside the library at the time, police said. Jeffrey Cassell, superintendent of Waynesboro Public Schools, praised the school's lockdown procedures and training, saying they "worked" in a time of crisis. THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN "Our safety and security protocols and procedures worked. Staff notified law enforcement immediately, and our school executed lockdown procedures. Every student and staff member is safe and returned home to their families," Cassell said. "If you don't get emotional today, you never will. Today is the day every school system hopes they never have to deal with," Cassell added, appearing to choke up. "Please hug your children and your families this evening." Ignatiadis-Isabelle had not attended any school in the district, Cassell told reporters. VIRGINIA UNIVERSITY REPORT FINDS OFFICIALS DID NOT DISCLOSE STUDENT’S TERROR CONVICTION Authorities did not share any details about an alleged motive, nor did they reveal anything about the weapon used or if the deceased gunman had a connection to the staff member who suffered a non-life-threatening gunshot wound. The identity of the staff member, who was treated and released from the hospital, has not been made public. Police emphasized multiple times throughout the press conference that the investigation remains active and ongoing. Five students were left injured and the suspect, 19-year-old Camron Harris, was arrested the same day after police said officers found him hiding in a closet inside one of the campus dorm buildings.

articles.title: Fundraiser for infant daughter of Erin Piacenti, stabbed to death in Times Square, triggers row as organizer is an Indian
articles.summary: US News: The fundraiser for Erin Piacenti triggered a massive row on social media, as one Shray Gupta organized it on behalf of the family for Erin's five-mont.
articles.body: The fundraiser for Erin Piacenti triggered a massive row on social media, as one Shray Gupta organized it on behalf of the family for Erin's five-month-old daughter, Madison. One Aman Gupta got trolled as an 'Indian scammer' as Aman shared the GoFundMe link from his X handle. "Our family is grieving after the horrific Times Sq attack this week. Please support Madison's future if you would like to help," Aman wrote. As people questioned the veracity of the fundraiser, Aman explained how he was related to the Piacenti family. But the trolling went on as many users questioned why the Piacenti family would need funds, as Madison's father, Frank Piacenti, is well-off."On August 31, Erin Piacenti, a beloved wife, mother, daughter, sister, and friend, was killed in a random, senseless, and unprovoked attack in Times Square. She was just 32 years old," the fundraiser said."Five months earlier, Erin and her husband, Frank, had welcomed their first child, Madison. Becoming a mother was Erin's lifelong ambition, and Madison gave her the greatest possible joy. August 31 was Erin's first day returning to work after her maternity leave.""Erin's life was defined not by the circumstances of her death, but instead by the way she lived. Erin was deeply devoted to her family and friends, exceptionally bright and accomplished, and was someone who brought warmth and energy to the people around her."The fundraiser gave details of Erin's education and career. "Erin graduated from the University of Pennsylvania, where she studied political science and sang in an a cappella group. She started her career as a buyer at Bloomingdale's. Erin later graduated from Fordham University School of Law magna cum laude, worked at Davis Polk for several years, and became a vice president at Bank of America," it said."Erin's career accomplishments, however, speak to only a small portion of who she was. To the people who knew and loved her, Erin was a thoughtful daughter and sister, a loyal friend, a devoted partner and companion in every aspect of Frank's life, and, most recently, an incredibly loving mother to Madison.""Erin and Frank celebrated their second wedding anniversary this summer, had just returned from a family road trip upon her passing, and were preparing to build a life together with their new daughter. That life changed incomprehensibly in an instant," it said.The fundraiser also said that the funds will be dedicated to supporting Madison "as she grows up surrounded by the family, friends, stories, and memories that will allow her to know just how remarkable her mother was."Is the fundraiser fake?Contrary to the social media trolling, there was no evidence that the fundraiser was fake. Shray Gupta said she is Frank's brother-in-law and the fundraiser was organized in consultation with Frank and Erin's family. Aman who shared the fundraiser and got called out as an Indian scammer, is Shray's brother.Indian-American Advocacy Council founder Rajeev Sharma condemned the attack on the fundraiser and said "proud patriots" were busy focusing on being racist instead of supporting the grieving family.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, Virginia bought 431 waterfront acres for a future state park; 21 years later, the undeveloped land has been folded into another park with a 30-year plan
articles.summary: US News: A 431-acre stretch of waterfront land in Gloucester County, Virginia, bought more than two decades ago to become a standalone state park, has official.
articles.body: A 431-acre stretch of waterfront land in Gloucester County, Virginia, bought more than two decades ago to become a standalone state park, has officially been added to nearby Machicomoco State Park under a newly approved 30-year master plan. The state bought the undeveloped property in 2005 for what was then planned as Middle Peninsula State Park. Located next to the historic Rosewell ruins, the land will now become Machicomoco’s "Western Unit". The change was formally approved in a master plan by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR) in February 2026, according to the Gloucester-Mathews Gazette-Journal. Despite the new plan, the land remains behind locked gates, with no public access and no fixed date for development. The entire master plan also faces a major challenge: no funding has been allocated for the work.Two decades of waiting along the York RiverThe story of the Western Unit began after a successful state bond referendum in 2002. Three years later, Virginia officials bought the 431-acre property, planning to turn the York River waterfront into the Middle Peninsula’s main state park. For years, the land remained untouched. The original 431-acre property and the land that later became Machicomoco both have strong historical links to the region. Both have large waterfront areas, were once homelands of the Powhatan confederacy, and were part of the large Rosewell plantation during the colonial period. Plans for the area changed significantly in 2018. A nearby 645-acre property known as Timberneck had once been planned for a housing development, with roads already built through the land. The Conservation Fund bought the Timberneck property in 2017, helping save it from commercial development. State officials approved plans for Machicomoco State Park the following year. Machicomoco opened in 2021 with hiking trails, camping areas, a day-use boat ramp, picnic shelters and educational exhibits focused on Native American history. The park welcomed more than 92,000 visitors in its first year and reached 114,617 visitors in 2023, according to figures in the DCR master plan. Meanwhile, the original 431-acre property remained closed and largely untouched.A three-phase vision spanning 30 yearsThe newly approved master plan sets out a 30-year development plan divided into three 10-year phases covering both park sites. However, DCR public communications manager Dave Neudeck told the Gazette-Journal that no state funding has been set aside or spent to carry out the plan. Phase 1 focuses on basic infrastructure and safety needs. At the Western Unit, proposed work includes improving waterfront safety, adding parking areas, building trails, providing ADA-compliant access to a picnic area and constructing a maintenance facility. At Machicomoco’s original site, known as the "Main Unit", Phase 1 would include adding electricity to existing yurts, creating trails through a longleaf pine management area, developing a native meadow viewshed, expanding parking and building a maintenance facility. The estimated cost of Phase 1 for both properties is $7,602,993 in 2024 dollars.Long-term plans depend on state fundingIf state lawmakers provide funding, Phase 2 and Phase 3 would bring larger developments. The master plan calls for a visitor centre, a nature-themed playground, a group campsite and a second full campground at the Main Unit. The Western Unit would receive a ranger residence and more trails. By Phase 3, planners hope to add a public fishing pier and picnic shelter at the Western Unit. The Main Unit would get a six-bedroom lodge, ten three-bedroom visitor cabins and more open outdoor areas and native meadows. Completing all three phases across both units over 30 years is expected to cost about $53.2 million in 2024 dollars. For now, signs on the gates of the Western Unit make clear that the public still has to wait. The vision laid out by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation depends entirely on future state funding. As Neudeck said about when the public might finally be able to enter the original 2005 purchase, development will move ahead only "if funding becomes available."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From busking in Stoke-on-Trent to supporting Sam Smith
articles.summary: Josie Oliver says she is "buzzing" with excitement to be opening for the Stay With Me singer.
articles.body:
When she was a teenager, musician Josie Oliver was performing in pubs and could regularly be seen busking in Stoke-on-Trent city centre.

Now, the 24-year-old singer-songwriter is preparing to support Sam Smith when they play at the London Coliseum on 16 September.

Oliver, from Stone, Staffordshire, was one of 10 up-and-coming artists who won the chance to open for Smith at their upcoming residency shows in Manchester and London.

She said she first heard of the competition, run by Smith and BBC Introducing, when her mother saw it and told her she would be "perfect for this".

"I just thought it was never going to happen but I did it anyway," Oliver told BBC Radio Stoke.

"Then I kind of forgot about it until I got the email through and I had to check it was real so many times because I was like 'surely not'."

She said she was "buzzing" for the opportunity, adding that it meant a lot, as an unsigned artist, to be given this kind of platform.

"It's such an incredible opportunity. I'm so excited."

Oliver has also been supported by BBC Introducing since first uploading her music in 2022.

Since then her tracks have been played more than 50 times and she has performed multiple sessions for BBC Introducing, including at The Complex in Burton and The Lexington in London.

Oliver said she had loved music for as long as she could remember, citing Genesis, Pink Floyd, James Blunt and Birdy among the artists she listened to while she was growing up.

She sang in her school choir, performed in pubs from when she was 14 years old and regularly busked in Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent, when she was a teenager.

She was also one of 10 third year students at the Liverpool Institute For Performing Arts selected to perform in front of Sir Paul McCartney.

Remembering the occasion, Oliver said it was "such a blur" and recalled how he had reassured her by telling her not to be nervous because they were "just sharing two songs".

For the competition to be one of the opening acts for Smith, she performed two new songs, including her single Killing Flies.

Oliver said the nerves were starting to kick in, but she was very much focusing on "the exciting part" at the moment.

"It's definitely the biggest thing I've done", she added. "Honestly [I'm] just rehearsing and I just have to trust that I know what I'm doing."

She said she had not spoken to Smith yet, but had been listening to their music since she was 12 years old.

"I have so many memories of singing their songs to karaoke so I would love to get a chance to speak to them."

articles.title: In 1880, Wisconsin’s Chippewa River became a 7-mile wall of logs as 200 million board feet of timber jammed the river before a flood broke it apart
articles.summary: US News: In the spring of 1880, a log jam of almost unimaginable scale formed on the Chippewa River near Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, stretching 7 miles from ban.
articles.body: In the spring of 1880, a log jam of almost unimaginable scale formed on the Chippewa River near Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, stretching 7 miles from bank to bank and lasting 6 weeks before it finally broke apart. Contemporary reports described a river transformed into a solid mass of tangled logs, so densely packed that a person could reportedly walk from shore to shore without ever once touching water. By some estimates, more than 200 million board feet of timber had piled up in the jam, making it the largest ever recorded on Earth at the time. The disaster grew out of the booming 19th-century lumber industry, which relied on floating felled trees downriver to sawmills, a system that occasionally produced jams when water levels dropped and logs became wedged together. This particular jam remains a Guinness World Records title today, one many experts believe will never be broken again.How the 19th-century lumber industry set the stage for the Chippewa log jamWhen lumberjacks first arrived in the American Midwest, they found a landscape almost entirely blanketed in forest, with Wisconsin alone holding an estimated 47,000 square miles of old-growth trees, an area roughly the size of England. Logging companies set up temporary camps along the region's rivers, felling trees and rolling them into the water to be floated downstream to sawmills. Workers known as river pigs or river drivers managed this flow using dams, booms and long hooked poles to steer logs and free them when they snagged, though variable water levels meant that occasional jams were an accepted risk of the trade. As reported in Why the record for longest log jam will probably never be broken and how it even happened, a contemporary newspaper account from The Saint Paul Globe on 31 May 1880 described the Chippewa jam as the largest ever known, with logs piled from bottom to surface across the river's full width.Why the log jam finally broke apart on 13 June 1880The jam held for weeks until a stretch of heavy rain in mid-June sent water levels surging. On 13 June 1880, dams at Yellow River and Point Creek gave way one after another, releasing floods of logs that had appeared securely fastened. According to a contemporary account from The Pantagraph published on 22 June 1880, the first rush alone carried around 150 million feet of timber downstream, with logs tumbling end over end and crashing in every direction as the flood pushed through the town. The surge of debris slammed into a covered bridge measuring 850 feet in length, tearing it from its piers and crushing it against the falls below, while townsfolk scrambled to build a temporary dam to keep the raging river from carving out an entirely new channel through Chippewa Falls.Why the 1880 Chippewa Falls log jam record may never be brokenThe scale of destruction left a lasting mark on Chippewa Falls, sweeping away large sections of the town even as it produced what remains, by volume, one of the most extreme log jams ever documented. In today's terms, 200 million board feet works out to roughly 471,947 cubic metres of sawn timber, comparable in size to a stack of planks covering a Manhattan city block and rising to half the height of the Empire State Building. A handful of large log jams occurred over the following decades, but none matched the scale of the Chippewa disaster, and as old-growth forests dwindled and logging shifted toward trucks, trains and mechanised methods, the conditions that produced such an event effectively disappeared. With modern forestry now focused on sustainable management rather than large-scale clear-cutting, the record set in 1880 looks set to remain unbroken for good.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Making too many life decisions around immigration timelines: Redditor says 'Canada does not owe me PR, coming back to India'
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At a time when the waiting line for a US Green Card is only getting longer, the situation in Canada is not very different either as a Redditor's post .
articles.body: At a time when the waiting line for a US Green Card is only getting longer, the situation in Canada is not very different either as a Redditor's post on coming back to India has gone viral. The Redditor came to Canada in 2023 and has been working in a managerial position in IT, but announced the decision to return to India on not getting Permanent Residency in Canada. The Redditor explained that they did everything by the book and really hoped to settle in Canada but offered the realization: Canada does not owe me PR. The post went viral as many social media users lauded the mature understanding of the situation and some also shared their similar experience."I came to Canada in 2023 and, like a lot of people, hoped I'd eventually be able to call this place home permanently. I didn't study here or come through some complicated route. I came here to work, had a good career and was fortunate enough to be very well compensated (way above what people are usually paid for my level and years of experience). I did everything by the book (maxed out all my scores with learning French being the only option left which I didn't want to pursue) and hoped that somewhere along the way there would be a realistic path to PR. It just never happened," the person wrote."I don't say that from a place of entitlement. Having a good job, paying taxes or contributing to the economy doesn't mean Canada owes me PR. But the immigration system can be incredibly frustrating when you're trying to plan a life around it. Scores change, programs change, draws change, rules change, and you keep wondering what the next announcement means for you. Eventually I realized I was making too many life decisions around permits, points and immigration timelines instead of what actually made sense for me and my family," the Redditor explained the decision to move back to India."I'm disappointed because I genuinely wanted Canada to work out, but I'm not leaving bitter. I've had some great experiences and got to see some ridiculously beautiful places. Seriously, Canada is unfairly beautiful sometimes. There are views from random road trips that I think I'll remember for the rest of my life. For all my frustrations with immigration, I'm genuinely grateful I got to live here. So that's it for me. No more CRS calculators, immigration announcements or wondering what the next draw will look like. Goodbye Canada. The PR dream wasn't meant to be, but I'm surprisingly okay with that," the post added.Why has getting Canadian PR become difficult?Under the 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan, Canada slashed its overall PR admission target to 380,000 per year. With over 100,000 fewer spots available per year, competition within the Express Entry pool is significantly intensified, keeping minimum Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) cut-offs consistently high. IRCC is in the process of replacing the classic three federal streams (Federal Skilled Worker, Canadian Experience Class, and Federal Skilled Trades) into a single consolidated class. The government is reviewing the 600-point boost traditionally given for a Provincial Nomination (PNP), as IRCC's targeted draws already capture similar profiles.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 24x7 eye on China, Pakistan borders: Why EOS-05 launch on 'Naughty Boy' is key to India's security
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: India is set to launch its first imaging satellite into geosynchronous orbit on Friday, with the EOS-05 mission expected to significantly s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India is set to launch its first imaging satellite into geosynchronous orbit on Friday, with the EOS-05 mission expected to significantly strengthen the country's ability to continuously monitor the same region of the Earth, including its borders and strategic areas.The state-of-the-art Earth observation satellite, also known as Gisat-1A, is scheduled to lift off at 2.55 am on September 4 aboard the GSLV-F17 rocket from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.ISRO has commenced the 27-hour countdown for the mission, which began at 11.30 pm on Wednesday. The 51.7-metre-tall GSLV-F17 is the 19th flight of India's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle.ISRO Chairman V Narayanan said all arrangements for the launch had been completed and described EOS-05 as a state-of-the-art Earth observation spacecraft that would strengthen India's Earth observation capabilities and improve the delivery of related services."Mr Narayanan said EOS-05 is a state-of-the-art Earth observation spacecraft and India’s first imaging satellite to be placed in a geosynchronous orbit. He said the mission will further strengthen India’s Earth observation capabilities and improve the delivery of Earth observation services."Satellite to keep constant watchThe key advantage of EOS-05's geosynchronous orbit is its ability to continuously observe the same region rather than capturing periodic images as satellites in lower orbits do.At an altitude of around 36,000 km, a geosynchronous satellite can match the Earth's rotation and remain over a fixed region. This enables near-continuous observation of areas of interest and allows rapid monitoring of events such as severe storms, lightning and fires.The capability could also strengthen surveillance of India's borders and other strategic areas by providing repeated and persistent imagery from space.Most of India's existing imaging and Earth observation satellites, including those in the Cartosat and RISAT series, operate in low Earth orbit. Such satellites move around the planet and may take days to revisit a location, depending on their orbit.EOS-05 carries two multispectral imagers. One of them has a spatial resolution of 42 metres per pixel, described as the highest resolution camera in a geostationary orbit.The satellite is designed for both civilian and strategic applications, providing detailed imagery and data for monitoring land, the environment and rapidly changing events.Mission follows 2021 setbackEOS-05 follows the failed launch of Gisat-1 in August 2021. The earlier satellite was lost when a technical anomaly in the cryogenic upper stage of the GSLV-F10 rocket prevented proper ignition.Had that mission succeeded, Gisat-1 would have become India's first Earth-imaging satellite to operate from geostationary orbit.The upcoming GSLV-F17 mission therefore marks a significant step in India's efforts to expand persistent Earth observation capabilities from geosynchronous orbit.Before the launch, Narayanan offered prayers at the Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple in Tirumala and placed models of the GSLV-F17 rocket at the feet of Lord Venkateswara.With the countdown underway, the launch is scheduled for 2.55 am on Friday from Sriharikota.

articles.title: US journalist gets 2-year prison term for working as Chinese government agent
articles.summary: US News: Texas-born journalist Thomas Weir Pauken II, 51, has been sentenced to two years in federal prison for acting as an undisclosed agent of the Chinese g.
articles.body: Texas-born journalist Thomas Weir Pauken II, 51, has been sentenced to two years in federal prison for acting as an undisclosed agent of the Chinese government in the US, the Justice Department said.Pauken, who pleaded guilty earlier this year, was also sentenced to 36 months of supervised release and barred from travelling overseas during that period. His lawyer, Charles Burnham, said Pauken has accepted the sentence and does not plan to appeal.Federal prosecutors said Pauken worked at the direction of individuals linked to China's government from at least 2019 until his arrest in February 2026. He received at least USD 100,000 for his work, which included writing reports and helping with efforts to recruit people who could provide sensitive information.According to court documents, Pauken worked with a person identified as "Cathy", who allegedly told him that his reports were being read by Chinese President Xi Jinping.He was also instructed to provide a potential recruit with a Samsung phone, computer and access to encrypted messaging platforms.Pauken moved to China in 2010 and worked for several Chinese media organisations, including state broadcaster CCTV. He later became an editor at Xinhua, China's state-run news agency, in 2024.US authorities said Pauken was stopped by Customs and Border Protection agents when he returned to the country in January 2025.During questioning, he acknowledged that he believed a person seeking a position in the Trump administration was likely to provide classified information to China, according to an FBI affidavit.However, his lawyer said the government acknowledged in court that Pauken did not provide any classified information to China.Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A Eisenberg accused Pauken of supporting Chinese Ministry of State Security operations, including recruitment and the gathering of sensitive information.Pauken, a Texas native, used the professional alias Tom McGregor while working as a commentator and writer in China. He also authored books on US-China relations and Shenzhen.The case comes amid a series of US prosecutions involving alleged Chinese government agents accused of operating in the country without making the required disclosures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Five African migrants dead after boat carrying over 100 people drifts for weeks in Atlantic Ocean
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At least five African migrants died after a boat carrying more than 100 people ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean while attempting to reach Spain'.
articles.body: At least five African migrants died after a boat carrying more than 100 people ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean while attempting to reach Spain's Canary Islands, authorities said on Thursday.Forty-four survivors were brought to safety after Spain's Maritime Rescue Service spotted the “precarious” vessel drifting south of Gran Canaria on Wednesday.Three survivors were evacuated by helicopter to a hospital, while the remaining 41 were taken by boat to the port of Arguineguín early Thursday and cared for by the Red Cross, news agency AP reported.Survivors say boat was adrift for nearly a monthAll the survivors were men, some of them underage, and were from Mali or Senegal, Red Cross spokesperson José Antonio Rodríguez Verona said.He said the migrants were disoriented and dehydrated, with many collapsing or vomiting after reaching land. Survivors said the boat had left Gambia and had been stranded at sea for “many, many days”, with some estimating they had spent nearly a month adrift.According to the survivors, the vessel had originally carried more than 100 people, including women and a baby. They said people began dying after the boat ran out of provisions and passengers fell ill after drinking seawater.Spain's Maritime Rescue Service said strong winds and waves up to 2.5 metres initially prevented rescuers from retrieving the five bodies found on board.NGO puts death toll at 83Helena Maleno, founder of migrant rights group Walking Borders, said 83 people had died during the voyage, including three women and a baby girl. She said the boat had left Gambia 27 days earlier.According to news agency AFP, Spain's maritime rescue service said it could not confirm the higher death toll, with a spokeswoman saying the other alleged victims had “not been found or rescued”.The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is considered one of the deadliest migration routes to Europe because of strong currents and the often overloaded vessels used for the crossing.5,163 migrants reached the Canary Islands by sea between January 1 and August 31, a 57% drop from the same period last year.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
articles.summary: The funeral of one of five young men killed in the crash with a police car is due to take place.
articles.body:
Four schools have said they will close early on Friday amid safety concerns over a funeral linked to a crash which killed seven people.

It is understood the funeral of Jakub Matusiak, 23, one of five young men killed in the head-on collision with a marked police car on the A66, is due to take place in Middlesbrough.

The crash happened near South Bank on 22 August when a Volkswagen Passat travelled the wrong way on the dual carriageway and hit a police car. Two police officers in the vehicle, PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were also killed.

Head teachers warned parents large crowds were expected to gather in the South Bank area for the funeral, with traffic disruption likely.

The decision to close the schools was taken following discussions between local head teachers and Redcar and Cleveland Council.

In an open letter, Conservative MP Laura Trott called on Education Secretary Lucy Powell to ensure the schools remain open.

The shadow education secretary also called for sufficient police support to be provided to keep schools in the area safe.

The Department of Education (DofE) has been contacted by the BBC for a response.

Cleveland Police said they were expecting the event to cause traffic disruption and delays, adding it had plans in place to ensure public safety.

South Bank Primary School and Outwood Academy Normanby are among the four schools which have confirmed they will close at lunchtime because of concerns about the impact of the funeral on pupils, staff and families.

Archway Academy in Teesville has confirmed it will close at 11:45 BST and St Margaret Clitherow's Catholic Primary School in South Bank at 12:15.

South Bank Primary School said it was closing early "to ensure the safety and wellbeing of our pupils".

Head teacher Tammy Cooper said large numbers of people were expected in the area for the funeral at St John's Church on Normanby Road.

The school also said some pupils might feel "upset or anxious" about the funeral and that its pastoral team would be available to provide support.

In a letter to parents, Mark Robinson, principal of Outwood Academy Normanby, said the school would also close early following discussions between local headteachers and the council.

Redcar and Cleveland Council said the Mackenzie Thorpe Centre will be closed all day and some SEND children who live in the South Bank area and attend other schools may be collected earlier in the day.

Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authority, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"As with any significant gathering, we have plans in place to ensure public safety and security, which is line with our usual process."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil, for one of the young men who died, last week was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash , according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

A total of 27 people have been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

articles.title: Sex offender ran into sea at Porthcawl to escape officers during arrest
articles.summary: Gavin Bennett is jailed for more than three years after running away from police during his arrest.
articles.body:
A sex offender who ran into the sea to escape being arrested has been jailed, South Wales Police has said.

Gavin Bennett, 45, ran into the water off Porthcawl, Bridgend County, at night after sending inappropriate messages to a girl he believed to be under 16.

In a video, two officers are seen wading into the Bristol Channel with torches at about 21:45 on 22 October 2025 and pulling Bennett out.

He was charged with two counts of attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child.

The force said he pleaded guilty at Cardiff Crown Court, and was sentenced on Tuesday to three years and eight months, and handed a 10-year sexual harm prevention order.

The sentence also covered two counts of sexually assaulting a female, relating to a separate incident spanning two years.

articles.title: Bid to withhold MI5 information from Heaton Park attack inquests
articles.summary: The Home Office wants the information withheld when the inquests take place next year.
articles.body:
The Government has applied to block some MI5 information relating to the fatal Manchester synagogue attack from being heard in public, a court has heard.

A pre-inquest hearing at Manchester Coroner's Court was told the Home Office wanted the information to be withheld when the inquests into the deaths of Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, are held next year.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in Manchester on 2 October last year.

He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt.

Cravitz died from multiple knife wounds while Daulby was killed by a bullet fired by armed police scrambled to the scene. He was hit as he blocked the synagogue doors to stop Al-Shamie getting in.

The hearing earlier was told by Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, that making public the information held by MI5 would put national security at risk.

He said: "The Secretary of State asserts that disclosure would harm national security."

But lawyers for the families of the victims said the Government's attempt to withhold the information, through a Public Interest Immunity application, was in "contradiction" to statements made after the attack.

The family lawyers cited statements made by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and counter-terror police bosses that terrorist Al-Shamie was not on their radar and unknown to them.

Victoria Ailes, representing the Cravitz family, told Judge Alexia Durran, Chief Coroner of England and Wales: "We would respectfully suggest the interest in open justice is heightened."

Anna Morris KC, representing the Daulby family, said there had been a "demonstrable lack of candour" by the security services in "other proceedings".

She said the Daulby family were also concerned that this application and information might contradict statements made publicly that the terrorist was not known to counter terror policing or the security services.

The Daulby family expected a "rigorous investigation" into his death and the family had concerns about any delay in proceedings and "procedural rights", she added.

Ed Pleeth, counsel to the inquest, told the hearing the PII application by the Home Office showed a "well-evidenced" risk to national security but the MI5 information was also relevant to the inquests that must take place.

He said in inquests there is no power to exclude certain parties, such as lawyers representing families or other parties, so the MI5 material could then not be heard.

Pleeth said the coroner must consider whether to convert the inquests into a public inquiry, where the law does allow sensitive security information to be examined in "closed" or private hearings attended only by a senior judge and security vetted lawyers.

Due to the "procedural uncertainty", no date has yet been set for the next pre-inquest hearing and a written ruling on the PII application is expected from the Chief Coroner at a later date.

Earlier, the Chief Coroner granted "interested person" status, meaning they will be legally represented at either the inquest or public inquiry, to three Greater Manchester Police firearms officers called to the scene, identified only as F42, S19 and C25.

The hearing was told officer F42 fired four times from his Glock pistol, with his first shot missing Al-Shamie and fatally hitting Daulby and injuring a second man, Yoni Finlay.

Officer S19 fired five times and C25 once, both using a "carbine" weapon.

Andrew Franks, who the court heard opened the synagogue compound gates to Al-Shamie, was also given interested person status, but the coroner said this did not imply any "criticism or culpability" on his behalf.

articles.title: She started streaming animals, then changed thousands of lives: Maya Higa’s journey from Twitch creator to conservation trailblazer
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Maya Higa did not set out to become one of the internet’s most distinctive conservation voices. Her path began with animals, moved through zookeeping .
articles.body: Maya Higa did not set out to become one of the internet’s most distinctive conservation voices. Her path began with animals, moved through zookeeping and Twitch, and eventually led to Alveus Sanctuary, a nonprofit built around rescued animals and online education. Today, her work is helping reshape how people encounter wildlife, proving that a livestream can do more than entertain. It can create curiosity, build empathy and inspire people to act.Maya Higa’s journey from zookeeper to Twitch creatorLong before thousands of viewers knew her name, Higa was simply a young woman who loved animals.She grew up on a farm surrounded by rabbits, horses, chickens and other animals. That early exposure shaped the direction of her life. At 18, while attending college, she took a job as a zookeeper. Her work also involved bringing animals such as kangaroos and lemurs to schools and birthday parties, where she could introduce children to wildlife in a direct and engaging way.Then Twitch entered the picture.Higa discovered livestreaming through friends who were broadcasting video games online. The idea was simple but powerful. Instead of speaking to a classroom or a small group at an event, she could potentially reach people anywhere.That opened a completely different door.Her content eventually developed around animals, education and conservation. The platform gave her something traditional wildlife education often struggles to achieve: an ongoing relationship with an audience.People could return. They could ask questions. They could watch an animal grow, recover or simply go about its day.That connection became the foundation for something much bigger.How Maya Higa built Alveus SanctuaryIn 2021, Higa turned her online audience into the driving force behind a far more ambitious project.She founded Alveus Sanctuary, a nonprofit that provides permanent homes for non-releasable animal ambassadors while using those animals to teach viewers about wildlife and conservation. Rather than treating the sanctuary as a place people must physically visit, Alveus brings the animals to audiences through livestreams and digital content.The idea sounds almost obvious now. At the time, it was a striking change in perspective.A traditional sanctuary has physical limits. There are only so many people who can visit, and frequent human interaction is not necessarily ideal for every animal.Alveus takes another route.Its cameras allow people to observe animals without requiring those animals to interact with a constant stream of visitors. The sanctuary describes its residents as ambassadors because their individual stories can help viewers understand the larger conservation challenges facing their species.The approach also helped transform online attention into financial support.Higa's 2021 fundraising livestream raised more than $500,000 to help establish the sanctuary. The campaign included a donor program and a live auction featuring items from other creators, showing how her growing online network could be converted into tangible support for animal welfare.That was an important moment. Higa was no longer simply creating content about animals. She was building infrastructure around the mission.Alveus Sanctuary turned viewers into conservationistsThe real strength of Higa's model is not the cameras themselves. It is the emotional connection they create.A person might know very little about an emu, hawk, parrot or amphibian. Give that animal a name and a personality, however, and suddenly the subject feels much closer.Alveus builds on that idea through educational programming such as Animal Quest. Each episode introduces an animal ambassador while exploring the animal's species, its place in the ecosystem, the threats it faces and what people can do to help.That distinction matters.The goal is not simply to make wildlife entertaining. It is to use entertainment as the starting point for learning.Higa has also leaned heavily into collaborations. Other creators can visit Alveus, learn about the animals and share that experience with their own audiences. The sanctuary says this approach has allowed collaborations to reach millions of people. In 2024 alone, more than 30 creators participated in collaborations, while the Alveus community contributed more than 9,000 hours to activities such as volunteering, trash collection and other efforts for the planet.Higa has described the value of that approach herself, saying, “I think it makes me a better educator.”It is a revealing comment. Her success is not built on separating education from personality. Instead, she uses the familiarity of a creator-led platform to make serious subjects easier for audiences to approach.Maya Higa’s conservation vision goes beyond the sanctuaryHiga's ambitions have now moved beyond caring for animals that cannot return to the wild.In her 2026 TED talk, she described her broader mission in simple terms: “My mission is to use the internet to build our next generation of conservationists.”That philosophy is shaping Alveus's next chapter.The organization says it is developing the Alveus Research & Recovery Institute, with plans to use conservation breeding programs to support species recovery and reintroduction. Higa's TED presentation highlighted critically endangered wolves as an initial focus.The ambition is significant because it changes the role of an online audience.A viewer is not expected to remain a passive spectator. The hope is that someone who first arrives because an animal is cute may eventually learn why its species is threatened, understand the forces behind that threat and decide to contribute in some way.That is where Higa's journey becomes more than a story about Twitch.It is a story about using attention differently.In 2026, WWF highlighted Higa's conservation work and her online community's participation in its Give an Hour for Earth campaign. WWF said her community had contributed tens of thousands of hours to the campaign the previous year.From a farm to a zoo, from a webcam to a sanctuary, Higa's career has followed an unusual path. Yet the central thread has stayed remarkably consistent: animals come first, education creates understanding, and understanding can lead to action.That may be the most important lesson in her rise. Higa did not abandon the internet to pursue conservation. She learned how to make the internet part of conservation itself.And with Alveus continuing to expand its educational and wildlife work, her most influential chapter may still be ahead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1997, Ted Turner opened his New Mexico ranch to endangered Mexican wolves; the facility became a major breeding centre for animals released into the wild
articles.summary: US News: In 1997, Ted Turner’s Ladder Ranch in south-central New Mexico became part of an ambitious attempt to rescue the Mexican wolf from extinction. Rather .
articles.body: In 1997, Ted Turner’s Ladder Ranch in south-central New Mexico became part of an ambitious attempt to rescue the Mexican wolf from extinction. Rather than treating his vast ranchland simply as private property, Turner helped create a wolf management facility where endangered animals could be housed, bred and prepared for a return to the wild. The Mexican wolf, a distinct subspecies of grey wolf, had been driven from much of its former range by persecution and predator-control campaigns. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says the last wild Mexican wolves were captured in the 1970s and used to establish a captive breeding programme. By 1998, wolves from that programme were being released in Arizona and New Mexico. Ladder Ranch became an important link in that process, providing a controlled setting where wolves could reproduce and acclimatise while retaining natural behaviour. Decades later, the facility remains closely tied to efforts to rebuild wild Mexican wolf populations across the Southwest today.How Turner’s private ranch became a conservation facilityThe Ladder Ranch Wolf Management Facility was established in 1997, the same year Turner and his family helped create the Turner Endangered Species Fund. According to TESF, it is one of three primary captive pre-release facilities in the Mexican wolf recovery programme. Animals can be housed, selectively bred and prepared for release, while wolves removed from the wild can temporarily return to managed care. TESF describes the facility as a “halfway house” between traditional captive facilities and the wild. Because Mexican wolves descended from a very small founding population, population growth and genetic management are central to recovery. Ladder Ranch became part of the conservation infrastructure needed to give wolf reintroduction a realistic chance for the recovery programme and reintroduction.The Mexican wolf had come dangerously close to extinctionThe Mexican wolf, Canis lupus baileyi, once ranged across parts of the southwestern United States and Mexico. Decades of persecution and government-sponsored predator-control programmes nearly erased it from the wild. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says wildlife biologists captured the last five remaining wild wolves to establish a captive breeding programme. The programme began with seven founding wolves. That history explains why every animal matters. Recovery requires increasing numbers without losing genetic diversity or behaviours needed for life in the wild. The Service says captive facilities manage reproduction so wolves selected for release retain genetic diversity crucial to success. Ladder Ranch gave conservationists another carefully managed place to breed, hold and prepare wolves for reintroduction across the Southwest.A long-term experiment in bringing a predator backThe work at Ladder Ranch has extended well beyond its original 1997 breeding role. According to AP News, the sprawling property spanning more than 243 square miles in southern New Mexico has worked with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for years, hosting not only Mexican wolves but a wider range of endangered-species projects run through the Turner Endangered Species Fund, from Bolson tortoises to black-footed ferrets and aplomado falcons. As reported by AP News, in 2021 the ranch took a further step by agreeing to host a translocated pack of wild Mexican wolves a mated pair and their pups moved from a wildlife refuge in central New Mexico to help boost the genetic diversity of the wild population. Federal officials told AP News the ranch's Seco Creek area, with its grasslands, pine forest and large resident elk herd, was chosen partly because of its distance from active livestock grazing allotments on the Gila National Forest.A partnership that has weathered controversyThat partnership has not been without friction. The ranch's role in the recovery programme has, at times, run into local political resistance. In 2015, New Mexico wildlife regulators declined to renew a permit in place for 17 years that had allowed the ranch to continue supporting the federal wolf programme. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said at the time that Ladder Ranch had been "an excellent partner in the recovery of Mexican wolves" and called itself "disappointed" in the commission's decision; the permit was later reinstated. Even so, the ranch has continued to serve as a site where wolves can be released into the wild or temporarily withdrawn from it, underscoring how a private ranching operation became, in AP News' account, an unusually durable piece of infrastructure in one of the country's most contested endangered-species recovery efforts.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Falkland Islands: Donald Trump hints US would not back UK over Argentina
articles.summary: The US president says the UK was not "there to help me" in his ongoing war with Iran.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.

"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'

Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.

He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".

Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands .

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
