articles.title: A Virginia mountaintop was scarred by coal mining; it now holds a 200,000-square-foot high school bringing students from four schools onto one campus
articles.summary: US News: A flat plateau once damaged by mountaintop removal coal mining has been given a new purpose as the site of a consolidated high school designed to beco.
articles.body: A flat plateau once damaged by mountaintop removal coal mining has been given a new purpose as the site of a consolidated high school designed to become an educational centre for central Appalachia. The newly built, 200,000-square-foot Southern Gap High School was officially opened during a ribbon-cutting ceremony in Buchanan County, Virginia, according to a report by the Virginia Mountaineer. The £60 million facility replaces four older local schools, bringing students from across the county together on one central campus built on a reclaimed ridge. Designed by VMDO Architects, the campus sits on land once used for heavy industrial activity. The project aims to respond to changes in the rural population and aging school buildings by bringing resources together in one modern facility.Transforming an extracted landscapeBuchanan County has long depended on coal mining, with mountaintop removal changing the area's landscape over several decades. According to project documents from VMDO Architects, the new school is intended to turn a former industrial site into a public space connected to the region's identity. The building's design reflects the county's coal-mining past. A long central brick corridor runs through the school and is designed to resemble the shafts of an underground coal mine. Metal-clad wings branch out from the main corridor, taking design ideas from the area's industrial history. The campus brings academic and practical subjects together under one roof. It includes engineering labs, large welding areas, college-preparatory classrooms, a performing arts auditorium and combined athletic facilities. Large windows along the main corridors offer wide views of the surrounding Appalachian mountains.Consolidating four rural campusesThe project brings four older school communities together into one school. Local leaders hope the shared campus will help reduce long-standing differences in resources and access across the rural county. By bringing students from different parts of Buchanan County together, Buchanan County Public Schools aims to give all students equal access to Advanced Placement courses, technical training programmes and modern sports facilities, regardless of where they live. During the opening ceremony reported by the Virginia Mountaineer, district officials described the project as an important long-term investment in local young people. Principal Mark Cooper called the opening a major moment for the county and said the school could become a central gathering place for a community moving beyond its industrial past. Superintendent Sherry Fletcher shared a similar view, describing the completed school as the result of a decade-long district plan to improve educational opportunities in rural Virginia.Infrastructure designed for regional retentionRural school districts across the United States continue to face problems linked to falling student numbers and people moving away for jobs. Local officials hope Southern Gap High School can also support economic development in Southwest Virginia. The campus is located near the Coalfields Expressway, which is still under construction, and forms part of a larger plan for the 2,000-acre Southern Gap plateau. The wider development is expected to include cultural attractions and commercial facilities. By bringing vocational training and college-preparatory education together, Southern Gap allows students to work towards trade certifications while also earning credits that can help with university admission. District leaders hope access to modern education and training close to home will encourage younger residents to stay in the area and build their careers locally. The school opened three days earlier than originally planned for the 2026 academic year after several years of construction work overseen by project managers Skanska and Buchanan County Public Schools. Classes for the newly combined student body are now underway.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Goethe Institute chief laments 'ending era' with last Russia closures
articles.summary: German-Russian cultural ties have reached the "end of an era," Goethe Institute President Gesche Joost said on Thursday after Moscow's decision to shut the o...
articles.body:
Goethe Institute President Gesche Joost laments the "end of an era" in German-Russian cultural ties as Moscow decides to close the organization's remaining centres in Russia amid Ukraine war tensions.

The closure of the Goethe Institute's centres in Russia follows the termination of the contract for the operation of the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin, suspected of fronting a spy network.

Berlin holds Moscow responsible for a recent drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announces sanctions against Russia, leading to expressions of regret from the German Cultural Council over the closure of the last three Goethe Institute centres in Russia.

German-Russian cultural ties have reached the "end of an era," Goethe Institute President Gesche Joost said on Thursday after Moscow's decision to shut the organization's remaining centres in the country amid Ukraine war tensions.

"For people in Russia who are learning our language and visiting our libraries, the end of our work there is bad news," said Joost, who has led Germany's worldwide cultural entity since November 2024.

This work in Russia had "already been increasingly restricted in recent years," according to Joost, noting that the number of staff had already been cut back since 2023.

This had left the remaining staff to carry out "vital work under the most difficult conditions," she said. The Goethe Institute now intends to discuss its next steps with the German Foreign Office.

According to the Interfax news agency, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov had announced the closure of its last three centres in Russia during a visit to Vladivostok on Thursday.

Earlier, news had emerged of the termination of the contract for the operation of the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin. Ostensibly there to promote Russian language and culture, the state-funded centre is suspected of fronting a spy network.

Berlin holds Moscow responsible for last month's attempted attack using an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport and has announced a list of sanctions against Russia, including the termination of the contract.

The German Cultural Council also expressed regret at the Russian decision to close the three centres in Moscow, St Petersburg and Novosibirsk.

"Now the very last doors to cultural exchange between Germany and Russia are being shut," said the council's executive director Olaf Zimmermann. "The Goethe Institute was one of the last seeds of exchange between the two countries."

articles.title: Civil war in Yemen continues to flare up with fresh attacks
articles.summary: Heavy fighting has broken out again in Yemen's Taiz province between the Houthi militia and troops loyal to the internationally recognized government, as the...
articles.body:
Heavy fighting has broken out in Yemen's Taiz province between the Houthi militia and government troops, escalating the civil war in the country.

The Houthis have attacked government troop positions along the Red Sea coast with rockets, leading to casualties among government soldiers and the downing of drones.

The conflict in Yemen has intensified with fresh airstrikes in the capital Sana'a, escalating fighting in multiple provinces, and threats to key shipping routes in the region.

Heavy fighting has broken out again in Yemen's Taiz province between the Houthi militia and troops loyal to the internationally recognized government, as the civil war intensifies against the backdrop of the Iran war, military sources said on Thursday.

The fighting saw the militia fire more than a dozen rockets at government troop positions along the Red Sea coast, according to military sources.

State-run broadcaster SABA reported "fierce fighting" on several fronts in the west of Taiz and that the army shot down several drones.

Several government soldiers were killed, according to local reports.

Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis have been fighting the Saudi-backed government for more than 10 years.

An unofficial ceasefire had been in place since 2022 and the war seemed to have reached a stalemate. There were no major skirmishes, but there was also no prospect of an end to the war.

"No war, no peace," was how British Yemen expert Helen Lackner summed it up.

Fresh airstrikes hit the Houthi-controlled capital Sana'a in July, and since then fighting has been escalating in Taiz and the provinces of Marib and Hodeidah.

The Houthis attacked targets including the port of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab (Gate of Tears) Strait, using rockets and drones.

Should the Houthis capture the city, they could intensify attacks on commercial shipping in the strait or bring traffic there to a halt using explosive-laden boats. The Bab al-Mandab, like the Strait of Hormuz, is a key shipping route for global trade.

In July, the militia announced a shipping blockade targeting Saudi Arabia. Since then, the Houthis have attacked at least three vessels, forced further ships in the region to change course and resumed strikes on southern Saudi Arabia.

Yemen is a deeply impoverished country on the Arabian Peninsula. The humanitarian crisis, which has been worsened by years of war, is among the most dire in the world.

More than 22 of Yemen's roughly 35 million inhabitants rely on humanitarian aid. All attempts to resolve the conflict through diplomacy have so far failed.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem passes away at 92: Hillary Clinton, Jill Biden, Meghan Markle, Lena Dunham and others remember the feminist icon who inspired generations of women
articles.summary: US News: Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist activist, author and journalist who became one of the most influential voices of the US women’s movement, has .
articles.body: Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist activist, author and journalist who became one of the most influential voices of the US women’s movement, has passed away at the age of 92. Following news of her death, tributes poured in from Hillary Clinton, Jill Biden, Meghan Markle, Lena Dunham, Roxane Gay, Rachel Cargle, Harvey Fierstein and several others who remembered her as a fearless trailblazer and a transformative force for gender equality.Steinem died peacefully on Wednesday at her home in New York City, surrounded by loved ones, according to a statement released by her representative on Thursday.“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the statement said. It also remembered her ability to listen to others and make people feel “seen and heard”, adding that her words, actions and example encouraged people to embrace their authentic selves.Hillary Clinton remembers Gloria Steinem as an architect of women’s equalityFormer US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton paid tribute to Steinem, recalling first becoming aware of her work during the 1960s and 1970s.Clinton said Steinem helped make the fight for equal opportunity more visible and connected the experiences of individual women to broader social inequalities. She credited the activist with helping build the movement for women’s equality and opening doors for millions of women who followed.Recalling Steinem’s influence on issues ranging from education and employment to reproductive rights and women’s participation in sports and politics, Clinton described her as an optimist whose activism was rooted in the belief that change was possible.“Be like Gloria: Embody possibility, and extend it,” Clinton said in her tribute shared on social media.Jill Biden says Gloria Steinem’s voice changed AmericaFormer first lady Jill Biden also mourned Steinem’s death, highlighting her decades-long fight for women’s equality and reproductive freedom.“Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures,” Biden wrote on social media.She praised Steinem for speaking up when it was difficult, listening to marginalised voices and continuing to push for change. Biden added that Steinem’s courage would continue to inspire future generations to defend the freedoms she spent her life advocating for.Meghan Markle remembers Gloria Steinem as friend and mentorMeghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, shared a deeply personal tribute to Steinem, posting photographs of the two together and remembering her not only as a feminist icon but also as a close friend and mentor.Markle recalled working alongside Steinem on initiatives encouraging young voters to participate in elections and discussing ways to make society more equitable. She also revealed that Steinem had spent Thanksgiving with her family and had offered her advice during difficult periods in her life.Reflecting on Steinem’s philosophy, Markle recalled the phrase “we are linked, not ranked”, which Steinem had shared with her. She also remembered a piece of advice Steinem once gave a young girl who did not know who she was: “It doesn’t matter if she knows who I am. What matters is that she knows who SHE is.”Markle concluded her tribute by thanking Steinem for the impact she had on generations of women.Lena Dunham recalls Steinem’s generosity and humourWriter and filmmaker Lena Dunham also paid an emotional tribute, describing herself as fortunate to have known Steinem personally.Dunham recalled how Steinem, despite her enormous responsibilities and global influence, made time for younger women and activists. She remembered visiting her home, receiving advice about relationships and activism, and witnessing her trademark humour.Dunham also recalled a recent gathering at Steinem’s home and a moment when the feminist icon spoke about watching ‘Call the Midwife’, a show centred on women helping other women.“You worked so hard for us. You gave so much,” Dunham wrote, adding that Steinem’s memory would continue to remind people of what was possible when society remained “linked, not ranked”.Writers and activists mourn feminist iconSteinem’s death also prompted tributes from writers, actors and social justice activists.Author Roxane Gay described her as “one of a kind” and praised her generosity, curiosity and thoughtfulness, calling her death a profound loss while pointing to the lasting power of her legacy.Social justice activist Rachel Cargle credited Steinem with inspiring her own activism, saying that she was forever grateful for what Steinem offered the world.Actor and playwright Harvey Fierstein remembered Steinem as an “unstoppable visionary” who demanded equal rights, political representation, reproductive freedom and equal pay. He also recalled working with her on the play ‘Bella Bella’, praising her generosity, intellect, historical knowledge and warmth.Gloria Steinem’s lasting legacySteinem became one of the most recognisable faces of the women’s liberation movement during the 1960s and 1970s. She advocated for reproductive rights, workplace equality and greater political representation for women.She began her journalism career in New York before becoming involved in the launch of Ms. magazine. She also helped establish the Women’s Action Alliance, an organisation dedicated to combating sexism.Over the decades, Steinem remained a prominent advocate for women’s rights and reproductive freedom. Her work and public life were later explored in the HBO documentary ‘Gloria: In Her Own Words’, which used archival photographs and footage alongside Steinem’s own recollections to chronicle the women’s movement through her perspective.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Stephen A Smith explains why he regrets voting for Harris, says her loyalty to Biden 'usurped everything else'
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith defended his Kamala Harris vote regret on Cari Champion and Jemele Hill's podcast as the hosts accused him of targeting Black women.
articles.body: ESPN's Stephen A. Smith was repeatedly confronted over why he said he regretted voting for former Vice President Kamala Harris during a podcast released Wednesday, as hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill suggested he was targeting Black women. "Flagrant and Funny" hosts Champion and Hill questioned Smith about his comments that he regretted supporting Harris in 2024 after he said it was the Democrats' plan all along to install her as the replacement for former President Joe Biden in the presidential race. Smith referenced the widely criticized moment from ABC’s "The View" on Oct. 8, 2024, when Harris appeared and said she couldn’t think of anything she’d do differently than Joe Biden. "Because when she went on 'The View' and she sat up there and said she couldn't think of anything that she would do differently, something that Sunny Hostin threw up intentionally as a softball for her to knock out the park. I'm like, when she passed up on that opportunity, this is not a dumb woman. This is a former state attorney general. This is a former senator. This is a former vice president of the United States. She is not dumb. There's only one reason she said that, because her loyalty to Joe Biden usurped everything else," Smith said. HUNTER BIDEN SAYS KAMALA HARRIS IS GETTING 'BAD POLITICAL ADVICE,' REFUSES TO EXPLAIN LOYALTY CRITICISM He added, "And I'm like, 'You trying to win a damn presidency? This is embarrassing. Do you want the presidency or don't you?'" Hill suggested Harris was trying to lean into Biden's accomplishments, and said, "He accomplished a lot." "But I understand when Sunny gave her that easy layup," Champion pressed. "But still, why was it necessary to say that you regretted voting for Kamala Harris when you knew that would take all of the hard work in which she tried to put together away from what she did?" Smith said he supported Harris throughout the election and that he made the comments afterward. STEPHEN A SMITH CALLS TRUMP AN 'UPGRADE' COMPARED TO BIDEN AMID NEW YORK KNICKS FEUD "I get where you're coming from, Cari, I really do. I think that it should have been far more upsetting if it was something that I said before the election. I did not. I supported her leading up to the election. I voted for her. I was on the airwaves talking about what it's going to take to win, win, win. And when it was over, I was honest about how I felt in the moment that that transpired," he said. Champion accused Smith of targeting Black women specifically and said he could have made his point about his criticisms without saying he regretted voting for Harris. STEPHEN A SMITH GOES OFF ON NATIONAL BLACK JOURNALISTS ORGANIZATION AFTER 'PERSONAL HIT JOB' AGAINST HIM Smith countered, "Can you concede that it's a disagreement as opposed to a disparagement?" She said she couldn't concede the point before the three turned to Smith's dispute with Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND Harris's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Curtis Houck, the managing editor of the Media Research Center's NewsBusters.org, told Fox News Digital, "This level of refreshing honesty from Stephen A. Smith has sadly been in short supply for far too long. Along with ideological diversity, more commentators and journalists should be willing to admit when they're wrong or express regret. The national media demand the utmost transparency and rigorous reflection from the people they cover, so why not have it go both ways?" Houck continued, "There's a reason why Smith is succeeding by moving outside his normal ideological bubbles. We need more of that from the ruling class, not less." During an April interview with Sage Steele, Smith was asked about his comments prior to the 2024 election on Dave Rubin's show about voting for Harris. "You went on his show, and you said that you voted for Kamala Harris?" Steele asked. "Yes," Smith responded. Steele then added, "And that you regretted it," to which Smith answered, "Yeah." Smith went on to explain that he cast that vote because he believed Harris was capable of compromise, but said he later concluded Democrats still did not understand why they lost. "I also believed that she was the kind of person that… could work across the aisle," Smith said. "And then when I saw how things were unfolding and how out in the clouds the Democratic Party was even after they lost the election, I just said, ‘There’s no hope.’" CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE In January 2025, Smith said during an interview with Bill Maher, "Yes, I voted for her, a lot of people voted for her, but in the end, we end up feeling like d--- fools, because we supported it. We fell for the okiedoke, as they say. If you had a primary, the likelihood is she would not have been the Democratic nominee." articles.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones uses Welsh accent in new Amazon series Kill Jackie
articles.summary: The Hollywood actress is starring in a new thriller series using her natural Swansea accent.
articles.body:
Catherine Zeta-Jones has been praised by fans as she uses her natural Welsh accent in an upcoming thriller series.

The 56-year-old Hollywood actor returned to her hometown of Swansea, where some of the filming took place for Amazon's Kill Jackie.

A trailer released on social media gives viewers their first glimpse of the show, as well as a snippet of Zeta-Jones using her Swansea accent.

The Oscar-winning star plays Jackie Price, an extravagant jet-setter who is trying to stay anonymous after escaping a "dangerous past as an international cocaine dealer," according to Amazon Prime.

One fan said they loved hearing the "queen of Wales sounding Welsh".

The series is based on the novel The Price You Pay by Nick Harkaway, published under his pseudonym Aidan Truhen.

Bilbao, Lisbon and London were also used as filming locations.

Zeta-Jones is known for an array of previous roles including Morticia Addams in Netflix's Wednesday, and an Oscar-winning supporting role in Chicago.

Kill Jackie will be her first major role using her Welsh accent.

She has previously spoken about her strong connection to Wales , adding in her heart she "never really left".

One fan commented on an Instagram post of the trailer, saying "her Welsh is out and I love it, can't wait".

Zeta-Jones said she had been looking forward to the opportunity to explore a female-driven plot that "encompasses empowerment, identity and redemption".

Damon Thomas, of Killing Eve, also stars in the show while Gangs Of London's Tom Butterworth is the writer and showrunner of the series.

Kill Jackie will premiere on 2 October on Amazon Prime

articles.title: In 1967, astronaut Vance Brand bought 160 acres beside Rocky Mountain National Park for $32,000; decades later, his family gave 40 acres to the park and Congress changed its boundary to accept it
articles.summary: US News: Former NASA astronaut Vance Brand spent decades exploring space and commanding shuttle missions, but a 40-acre piece of land along the eastern boundar.
articles.body: Former NASA astronaut Vance Brand spent decades exploring space and commanding shuttle missions, but a 40-acre piece of land along the eastern boundary of Rocky Mountain National Park remains one of his most lasting contributions on Earth. The story began in 1967, when Brand bought 160 acres of land next to the national park for $32,000. Decades later, with the support of his wife and children, he decided to donate a quarter of the property, 40 acres of undeveloped forest, to protect the natural landscape around the park. The land was first transferred in 2019 to the Rocky Mountain Conservancy, the non-profit partner of the national park, to hold until federal officials could officially add it to the park. Because changing the boundary of a national park requires federal approval, Congress had to act. In 2020, Colorado lawmakers introduced the Rocky Mountain National Park Boundary Modification Act. The legislation was sponsored in the Senate by Senator Michael Bennet and former Senator Cory Gardner, along with Representative Joe Neguse in the House. It quickly gained bipartisan support, passed through Congress and was signed into law in January 2021, officially changing the park boundary.Expanding protected high-elevation ecosystemsIn September 2022, officials from Rocky Mountain National Park, the Rocky Mountain Conservancy and the Brand family gathered near the park boundary for a formal ribbon-cutting ceremony. The event marked the final addition of the 40-acre property to the federally protected park. According to official National Park Service news releases, the land sits next to the park's eastern boundary, about four miles from Longs Peak. The property is covered by aspen and pine forests and crossed by small mountain streams. It creates a natural buffer between private homes and three popular hiking routes: the Estes Cone, Storm Pass and Eugenia Mine trails.In a statement released by the National Park Service, Brand explained why he chose to donate the family property: "To me the park is a wonderful place that must be preserved – and where possible expanded. The numerous hiking, camping, and (non-technical) mountain climbing experiences that I had there in my youth led me to purchase land along Rocky Mountain National Park's eastern boundary in 1967. Over time my family has developed an appreciation of the natural beauty of the land and have encouraged keeping it as it is. I'm thankful that there were early national park enthusiasts like Enos Mills and Teddy Roosevelt who had the foresight to encourage establishment of Rocky Mountain National Park and our entire national park system. The National Park Service does a terrific job of maintaining our national parks. In short, my family and I sincerely hope that this donation to the national park will keep the land in its natural state for the benefit and enjoyment of current and future generations of Americans."From boyhood hikes to orbitBrand was born and raised in Longmont, Colorado, where the tall peak of Longs Peak stood above the western skyline. As a Boy Scout and later a student at the University of Colorado Boulder, he spent summers working different jobs in Estes Park. He worked as an elevator operator at the historic Stanley Hotel and as a busser at the Plantation Cafe, while spending his free time hiking local trails. After finishing his studies, Brand became a Marine Corps officer, military pilot, test pilot and aeronautical engineer before joining NASA. In 1975, he served as the command module pilot on the historic Apollo-Soyuz Test Project, the first joint spaceflight between the United States and the Soviet Union. He later commanded three Space Shuttle missions: STS-5 in 1982, STS-41-B in 1984 and STS-35 in 1990.Despite travelling into low Earth orbit, Brand kept a strong connection to the wilderness where he grew up. In interviews with regional news outlets, including CBS Colorado and The Denver Post, Brand described buying the land as a fortunate investment that he was happy to return to the public. When lawmakers considered expanding the park boundary, they stressed that the donated property would not create an added financial burden for the federal park system. In letters to Congress, Rocky Mountain Conservancy Executive Director Esther Rivera Murdock said the land was completely natural and undeveloped, meaning park staff would not face deferred maintenance costs after it was added.Federal funding and conservation managementThe land transfer is recorded in official government reports covering conservation work on public lands. In the Fiscal Year 2022 Lands Accomplishments Report published by the Land and Water Conservation Fund under the National Park Service, federal officials described the Brand donation as an important success for public land management and wildlife habitat connections. According to the Land and Water Conservation Fund report, protecting buffer areas around high-elevation ecosystems helps preserve wildlife corridors used by animals moving between different elevations as seasons change. Bipartisan action in Congress allowed the land to become part of the park without using federal land acquisition funds, helping protect sensitive habitats at no cost to taxpayers. Representative Joe Neguse, whose district includes the park, said during congressional testimony that expanding Rocky Mountain National Park protects important wilderness areas for millions of visitors each year while preserving the natural condition of the surrounding mountains. The property is now permanently managed by the National Park Service. For the millions of visitors who use the Estes Cone and Storm Pass trails, the former astronaut's 40-acre donation means the forests along the eastern side of the park will remain protected and largely undisturbed for generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At 15, Jim Bishop bought 2.5 Colorado acres with $450 he earned mowing lawns and delivering papers; 10 years later, he began a stone castle that he spent 50 years turning into the world’s largest one-man project
articles.summary: US News: Nestled in the Wet Mountains of Colorado, at an elevation of 9000, is the world's largest one-man project, The Bishop Castle. From 1969 to 2019, the m.
articles.body: Nestled in the Wet Mountains of Colorado, at an elevation of 9000, is the world's largest one-man project, The Bishop Castle. From 1969 to 2019, the monument was constructed by one man, all by himself, James Roland Bishop, also known as Jim Bishop, the Castle Builder, according to the website.Laying the foundationJim Bishop had always been captivated by the majestic mountains rising up to the southwest of Pueblo, where he grew up. One fine day in 1959, while he was riding bicycles with friends along a mountain road in the San Isabel National Forest, Jim found a small slice of heaven tucked away at an elevation of 9,000.This 2 1/2 acre parcel of land was surrounded by national forest on three sides. While working with his father Willard in the family ornamental iron business and also doing side gigs mowing lawns and delivering newspapers, the 15-year-old had put away $450 in savings. Since he was too young to buy the land himself, he convinced his parents to buy it for him, using his savings.For the next ten summers, Jim and his father camped out on the land and prepped the area for the construction of a family cottage. This experience exposed Jim to a peculiar affinity for hands-on work, such as swinging an axe and wielding a shovel. In June of 1969, he and his father began building a rock cottage, which included a water tank surrounded by a rock wall and some arched windows. Friends and family would come up to visit, and many of them commented that it looked like a castle. By 1972, rumours had spread in the local communities of a castle being built near San Isabel in Colorado.This planted the idea in Jim's mind and it swiftly took root. The next spring in 1973, Jim began digging a hole down to bedrock out in front of the cottage to be. When Willard asked “Jim, what are you doing now?”, Jim replied, “The people want a castle and I’m gonna’ build them a castle!” Willard threw his hands up and said “That’s just too much work! We came to the mountains to get away from people, and now you want to build them a castle?”Why a castle?Eventually, Jim dropped out of high school after an argument with one of his teachers who told him, "You'll never amount to anything Jim Bishop!" And history holds true to the fact that it is mostly these students whose teachers have told them that they wouldn't be able to do something, who truly make it in life.For Jim, the comment sparked a fire to prove his teacher wrong. The words inspired him to do something grand, something the world hadn't seen yet. As people would come to see him working on the castle, many doubted if he would be able to complete it alone. “What are you doing Jim? You’re never going to pull this off!” they would tell him.In one interview, he declared, “I want to see how long I can live and what I can build with my hands… It drives me on. It makes me say ‘Oh ya? You say I can’t do this? Well watch me!’”But Jim was never a man of wealth, so how did he manage to build the castle? Early in the Castle’s construction, Jim funded the project with his own money, a sacrifice that he believed would be worth it in the long run. Eventually, he decided to begin accepting donations. Despite many people’s suggestions that he could be making a lot of money on the place, he did not want to charge admission or allow the place to become a tourist trap.He always welcomed people to visit and tour the castle without charging them any kind of fees or dues. He only asked that they donate what they could afford and he would build as much as the visitors provided for.A legacy for lifeIn 2019, Jim unknowingly did the last work on his monument, setting small rocks into place along parts of the Great Wall, without using any concrete, as he was physically incapable of mixing mortar and hauling it in buckets. “I pray to God every day that I get back to my old self”, he said in an interview, as Parkinson’s Disease had robbed him of his strength little by little. However, he continued to welcome visitors, answer questions, and tell stories every chance he had. He often reminisced about his “gal” Phoebe, who had passed away in 2018, and shared photos of her with everyone he met.His son Daniel and daughter-in-law Sage took care of him for several years, even moving into his home to care for him. One day in 2023, after landing in the hospital for a bout of dehydration, it was decided that a long-term care facility would be in his best interest.As his health deteriorated, Jim found peace in the fact that his son was the Castle Caretaker now, and would ensure his legacy continued the way he wanted. On November 21, 2024, Jim Bishop passed away, surrounded by loved ones, and assured that his gift to the world would remain long after his time here on earth. Daniel Bishop now cares for his father’s work and has been the Castle Caretaker since about 2018, when his mother passed away and his father’s health began to decline more rapidly. Daniel plans to keep his father’s legacy alive, and even has plans to finish Roy’s Tower, among other projects on the property.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Artist creates cars filled with water to show tide in Plymouth
articles.summary: David Cotterrell's installation has the water level in the cars change in tune with the tides.
articles.body:
An art installation made up of cars filled with water has been created to illustrate the rise and fall of the tide.

Artist David Cotterrell has repurposed four old Ford Fiestas and filled them with water, the level of which will rise and fall in response to tidal information in Plymouth.

He said: "There's something wonderfully strange about encountering an ordinary car and realising that it is quietly responding to the sea."

The cars will be on display at Tinside Lido, Mount Batten, Tavistock Place and Mount Edgcumbe from Thursday, before they are moved to other parts of the city during September and October.

Cotterrell said: "We live alongside the tide, but it's remarkably easy to stop noticing it.

"I wanted to take that familiar rhythm and place it somewhere it doesn't belong – inside an object we barely give a second glance."

He removed the 25-year-old cars' engines and conventional operating systems and installed tanks, pumps, electrical systems, sensors, filtration, software and bespoke engineering.

Plymouth Culture said as the tides changed, water would move between a hidden reservoir and the visible cabin to create an "unexpected fragment of an intertidal environment within the city".

Cotterrell said he hoped the cars would make people "pause, look again and perhaps notice the connections between Plymouth and the water that's all around us".

The installation, called Intertidal, is part of the Sea for Yourself programme led by Plymouth Culture in partnership with Plymouth Sound National Marine Park and Plymouth City Council.
